--- ABSTRACT ---
[STUDY DESIGN]: A descriptive case review.
[OBJECTIVES]: To assess the outcomes of anterior lumbar interbody fusion for painful discs within a solid posterolateral spinal fusion.
[SUMMARY OF BACKGROUND DATA]: Some patients continue to have pain after posterolateral spinal fusion despite apparently solid arthrodesis. One potential etiology is pain that arises from a disc within the fused levels.
[METHOD]: Retrospective review of 176 patients with anterior interbody fusion, which located 20 who had anterior interbody fusion levels of prior posterolateral spinal fusion. All had low back pain, solid posterolateral spinal fusion, and painful disc(s) at the posterolateral spinal fusion level(s) but not elsewhere. Pain was measured by the Numerical Rating Scale, function by Oswestry Disability Questionnaire, and patient satisfaction by the North American Spine Society Outcome Questionnaire.
[RESULTS]: Follow-up data were available for 18 patients (90%). Mean follow-up was 58 months (25 to 102). There were 10 men and 8 women. Mean age was 45 years (26 to 72). Diagnoses were degenerative discs, herniated nucleus pulposus, spondylolisthesis, and spinal stenosis. Eight patients had injuries after the previous posterolateral spinal fusion that precipitated new symptoms. Two patients had one level fusion, 14 had two levels, and 1 each had three and four levels. Four patients had one prior surgery, 5 had two, and 9 had three or more. All patients had solid anterior interbody fusion by radiograph. Mean Numerical Rating Scale improved from 7.9 before surgery to 4.7 after (P< 0.001). Mean Oswestry Disability Questionnaire improved from 56.3 before surgery to 47.9 after (P = 0.04). Of 15 patients unable to work before anterior interbody fusion, 5 returned to work. Sixteen patients (89%) were satisfied with their results.
[CONCLUSION]: Low back pain that continues or recurs after apparently solid posterolateral spinal fusion may be caused by painful disc(s) at motion segment(s) within the fusion. A solid posterolateral spinal fusion may not protect the residual disc(s) from injury. Anterior interbody fusion can provide significant improvements in pain and function and a high degree of patient satisfaction in this clinical setting.

key_findings.finding: The strongest direct study is a retrospective descriptive case review of 176 ALIF patients that identified 20 patients with painful disc(s) within a radiographically solid prior posterolateral fusion; 18 had follow-up (mean 58 months, range 25–102). Mean pain score improved from 7.9 to 4.7 (P<0.001), Oswestry Disability Questionnaire from 56.3 to 47.9 (P=0.04), all had solid anterior fusion by radiograph, 5/15 unable to work returned to work, and 16/18 (89%) were satisfied. This directly supports salvage anterior interbody fusion for same-level residual discogenic pain despite solid posterolateral arthrodesis, but is low-level evidence without a control group and with limited complication reporting.

source_tools.relevance: Direct clinical study abstract and extracted results

key_findings.finding: A 2023 retrospective level-IV series of 22 patients undergoing ALIF plus posterior instrumentation for revision lumbar interbody fusion reported mean follow-up of 73 months (20–121); 50% reached the MCID for back-pain improvement, 64% for leg-pain improvement, and 73% had excellent/good modified MacNab outcomes. Pain and lumbar lordosis improved significantly, but ≥2 preoperative fusion segments predicted poorer back-pain response. This supports ALIF as a potentially effective revision strategy, although it is not a clean study of isolated prior posterolateral fusion or discogenic pain and therefore should not be equated with the direct same-level PLF evidence.

source_tools.relevance: Revision ALIF cohort outcomes and follow-up

key_findings.finding: The available searches did not identify a robust comparative trial or sizable dedicated cohort specifically evaluating anterior revision/salvage fusion for same-level pseudarthrosis after prior posterolateral-only fusion. The 2023 revision ALIF cohort included revision interbody-fusion patients and collected pseudarthrosis as a factor, but the retrieved data do not provide a separate pseudarthrosis subgroup fusion rate or complication rate.

source_tools.relevance: Revision ALIF search results and cohort characterization

key_findings.finding: Adjacent-segment disease is a distinct indication from same-level painful residual disc or pseudarthrosis. The adjacent-segment search mainly returned biomechanical, risk-factor, and non-ALIF revision literature; it did not yield direct clinical evidence establishing that ALIF at a previously fused level improves pain from adjacent-segment disease. Therefore, the positive 2000 study should not be generalized to adjacent levels.

source_tools.relevance: Direct same-level study explicitly limited painful discs to prior PLF levels and excluded pain elsewhere

key_findings.finding: Overall conclusion: anterior lumbar fusion—particularly ALIF—can improve pain and function when a residual painful disc is demonstrated within a solid prior posterolateral fusion, with the best direct evidence showing durable improvement over approximately 5 years and radiographic fusion. Evidence for revision of nonunion/pseudarthrosis after posterolateral fusion and for adjacent-segment disease is substantially thinner, heterogeneous, and insufficient to claim a predictable benefit; complication data are incompletely reported in the direct study.
